clinicalPearls: The most severe form of the exstrophy-epispadias complex, in which an exstrophied segment of hindgut/caecum lies between two exstrophied bladder halves on the lower abdominal wall
Frequently occurs as the OEIS complex: Omphalocele, Exstrophy of the cloaca, Imperforate anus, and Spinal defects

Associated anomalies are the rule and include omphalocele, imperforate anus with a foreshortened or blind-ending hindgut, spinal dysraphism and tethered cord, and skeletal, renal, and genital anomalies
Genital anomalies are marked; in males the phallus is often bifid or diminutive, historically raising complex questions of gender assignment now guided by multidisciplinary DSD care
Because of the visceral and neural involvement, management is far more complex than for classic bladder exstrophy
Neonatal care requires a coordinated team addressing the omphalocele, bowel diversion, staged closure of the exstrophy, and neurosurgical assessment of any spinal cord lesion
Long-term goals include urinary and faecal continence (often via reconstruction and stomas), preservation of renal function, and attention to sexual and psychosocial outcomes
reference.pathophysiology: Cloacal exstrophy results from a very early and extensive developmental failure of the lower abdominal wall, in which an abnormal, prematurely disrupted cloacal membrane and defective mesenchymal migration occur before the urorectal septum has divided the cloaca. As a result the bladder is split into two halves that flank an exstrophied central plate of hindgut, and the anus is imperforate. Because the insult occurs so early and involves the cloaca, associated omphalocele, spinal dysraphism, and genital and skeletal anomalies are common, reflecting a global disturbance of caudal embryonic development rather than an isolated urinary tract defect.
additionalInvestigations: Renal and abdominal ultrasound to assess the upper tracts and associated anomalies
Spinal ultrasound and MRI to detect dysraphism and tethered cord
Echocardiography and skeletal imaging for associated anomalies
Karyotype and multidisciplinary DSD evaluation to guide gender and genital management
Contrast studies of the bowel to define hindgut anatomy
redFlags: Neonatal instability from the omphalocele, exposed viscera, or associated cardiac disease
Progressive neurological deficit from a tethered or dysraphic spinal cord
Upper-tract obstruction or deteriorating renal function
Sepsis from exposed bowel and bladder plates or after reconstruction
reference.prognosis: Survival has improved markedly with modern neonatal and staged surgical care, but children face multiple reconstructive operations and lifelong management of urinary and faecal continence, renal function, spinal and orthopaedic issues, and sexual and psychosocial development, so outcomes remain guarded and highly individual.
pitfalls: Treating it as a more severe bladder exstrophy while overlooking the bowel, spinal, and genital components
Missing occult spinal dysraphism or tethered cord that needs neurosurgical input
Making premature or unilateral decisions on gender assignment outside a multidisciplinary DSD framework
Failing to coordinate the many specialties required for staged reconstruction
management: Neonatal stabilisation with protection of the exposed bladder and bowel plate and management of the omphalocele.
Staged surgical reconstruction of the exstrophy including bladder closure, often with pelvic osteotomy to approximate the pubic bones.
Bowel diversion with colostomy while preserving all available hindgut, with later consideration of pull-through or a permanent stoma.
Neurosurgical assessment and repair of associated spinal dysraphism and tethered cord.
Multidisciplinary disorders-of-sex-development care to guide gender assignment and staged genital reconstruction, informed by karyotype.
Long-term surveillance of renal function and the upper tracts, with continence achieved through clean intermittent catheterisation, bladder augmentation or urinary diversion as needed.
Coordinated multidisciplinary team management across paediatric surgery, urology, neurosurgery, orthopaedics and nephrology, with psychosocial support for child and family.
